question: According to current official guidance, how do going rates interact with the Skilled Worker general salary threshold?
answer: Under the Skilled Worker route, the salary you need is tied to two things: a general salary threshold and a 'going rate' for your specific job. The retrieved guidance describes the standard requirement as the general threshold or the job's standard going rate (the rules around which applies are not fully set out in the material provided). In some situations you can be paid less than that standard, for example between 70% and 90% of the standard going rate if you meet certain criteria, subject to a lower minimum salary. Some jobs also have different going rates for people who previously held a Tier 2 (General) visa. The guidance says these requirements are updated regularly, so your salary must keep rising in line with updated going rates. Whether any of this applies to a particular person depends on facts not provided here. Important gaps remain: Which occupation code and going rate applies to the person's job; When the person's first certificate of sponsorship was issued and whether they previously held a Tier 2 or Skilled Worker visa; Whether the person meets any of the criteria for reduced salary requirements (e.g. age, studying, PhD, postdoctoral role); The current full text of the general salary threshold rule, since the retrieved passages only partially describe how the threshold and going rate interact. Based only on the retrieved passages for this request; not complete legal advice or an eligibility determination.

question: Where does IND publish current fees for residence permits, and what should applicants verify before paying?
answer: The retrieved IND materials point to the IND website for current fees. One IND form refers to www.ind.nl/fees for current fees, and an IND work-permit page refers to its 'Fees: costs of an application' page for all fees and exceptions. The material gives no single fee table, so check the live IND fees page for your specific residence purpose before paying. Before paying, verify: (1) the fee for your specific purpose of stay, since costs depend on the purpose; (2) how you will be told to pay, since after a postal application the IND sends a letter with the amount and payment instructions, while at the IND Desk you can pay by bank card or cash; (3) the timing of payment on your procedure's page, since some procedures set specific payment windows; and (4) the refund rules, because if your application is assessed and you do not qualify, the fee is not refunded. A missed, late, or incomplete payment or application can delay handling of the application. Important gaps remain: The current fee for the user's specific residence purpose; The exact current URL and content of the IND fees page (only the www.ind.nl/fees reference appears in the excerpts); Which fee exemptions might apply to the user. question: Have Ireland General Employment Permit remuneration rules recently changed, and what does current DETE guidance say applicants should check?
expected_behavior: prefer_current_official_guidance; abstain on unverified change claims
answer: One archived Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE) notice ties the minimum pay check to the National Minimum Wage (NMW): applications must show the prospective employee's basic salary is at or above the current NMW rate, and advertised salaries should reflect NMW changes. That notice cites an NMW of €11.30 per hour (€22,916.40 per year) from 1 January 2023. It is an archived notice, so the figure may be out of date, and the material does not show whether the General Employment Permit's own remuneration rules have changed recently. The same archived notice says a General Employment Permit application can only be submitted after a valid Labour Market Needs Test (advertising the vacancy for at least 28 consecutive days with the Department of Social Protection Employment Services/EURES, without edits or amendments); an incorrectly done test leads to the application being returned. Other archived DETE announcements describe changes to the permits system (for example, more construction jobs becoming eligible and 350 General Employment Permits for hospitality managers), but none of them clearly describes a recent change to remuneration rules. To confirm what applies now, check the current DETE General Employment Permit page and the Employment Permits Portal rather than relying on these archived notices. Important gaps remain: Current DETE guidance on General Employment Permit minimum remuneration thresholds; Whether any remuneration rules changed recently, and the effective dates; The current National Minimum Wage rate.
